notes: Airbus, which built the satellite, says it provides connectivity over Europe, the Middle East, Africa and central Asia, in C and Ku band. That is nearly everything in its line of sight, which is why the line of sight alone says little about where a beam points.

Arabsat publishes contour files for this satellite behind the Badr-8 page of its website (KML, downlink EIRP in dBW: six Ku-band beams and a C-band global beam). They were read on 24 Nov 2026 for where the contours run, and are redrawn here with credit; no file is copied. Arabsat's terms ask that its site not be linked without consent, so it is credited by name only.
Uplink and downlink beams are different shapes on most satellites. Only downlink beams are named in the public material found.

cases.title: High-throughput GEO: KA-SAT
cases.summary: A Ka-band satellite at 9 degrees east that covers Europe and the Mediterranean with about 82 small spot beams instead of a few large ones. The public record gives the number of spots, a round figure for their size and the region in words. Where each spot sits is on the operator's map, which may be linked but not redrawn.

layers.label: Line of sight: the satellite is 10 degrees or more above the horizon
layers.source: Orbit's GEO day file (element sets: Space-Track.org, USSPACECOM)
layers.uncertainty: Position to a few km; the outline to well under 0.1 degree. Terrain and buildings not included.

layers.label: Line of sight: the satellite is 5 degrees or more above the horizon
layers.source: Orbit's GEO day file (element sets: Space-Track.org, USSPACECOM)
layers.uncertainty: Position to a few km; the outline to well under 0.1 degree. Terrain and buildings not included.

layers.label: One spot beam, for scale: one spot as a cone 0.46 degrees wide at the satellite, which is 300 km across where it is aimed (Rome, as an example only)
layers.source: Eutelsat's own 2012 presentation gives about 300 km across for each spot; another technical page gives 0.5 degrees
layers.uncertainty: A round published figure with no gain level; sources give 250 to 300 km. The aim point is an example, not a real beam centre, so this shows the size of a spot and nothing about its place.

layers.label: Whole service area, from the words 'Europe and the Mediterranean Basin': smallest ellipse, as the satellite sees it, around the mainland and nearby islands of 48 European and Mediterranean countries (between 12 west and 45 east, 27 and 72 north), as Orbit read the phrase (3.763 by 2.093 degrees half-axes)
layers.source: Service area in words from public descriptions of KA-SAT; the country list is Orbit's reading
layers.uncertainty: An outline around named countries. Spot-beam satellites leave gaps inside such an outline (sea, desert, unserved countries), which this cannot show. Not checked against any published contour.

notes: No published contour exists here to check the estimates against, so they carry no score.
Sources give 82 or 83 spot beams; two of the beams are said to be alternatives to each other.

KA-SAT was Eutelsat's and is now owned by Viasat (through Euro Broadband Infrastructure). Blackout's register reaches it through Skylogic's networks, which run its gateways. A network number therefore does not name the satellite's owner.
On a spot-beam satellite a user's outage can come from one spot or one gateway. Neither can be placed from public data without the operator's beam map.
No contour for this satellite was found in a public filing: it is not US-licensed, and ITU's beam data needs a login that Orbit does not use.

cases.title: LEO constellation: Starlink
cases.summary: A low-orbit constellation has no fixed footprint. From orbits alone, the only thing that can be computed is how many satellites stand high enough in the sky at each latitude. Where service is actually sold and switched on is set by licences, gateways and the operator, and has to come from what the operator publishes or from terminals seen in use.

layers.label: Satellites above the service angle of 25 degrees (5 degrees from 62 north), mean over 24 hours, by 2-degree latitude band (heavier shading is more)
layers.source: CelesTrak, Starlink group (element sets from the 18th Space Defense Squadron)
layers.uncertainty: Geometry only: no gateways, licences, capacity or terminals. Spherical Earth; a few km at band edges.

layers.label: Where the 9,458 serving satellites were at 2026-11-24 16:00 UTC
layers.source: CelesTrak, Starlink group (element sets from the 18th Space Defense Squadron)
layers.uncertainty: SGP4 from public element sets: about 1 km at the set's epoch, growing by a few km a day.

layers.label: Terminals seen in use: RIPE Atlas probes connected through Starlink's network (AS14593), at the places their hosts report (127 points, 41 countries)
layers.source: RIPE Atlas probe API (RIPE NCC)
layers.uncertainty: A lower bound from volunteers, mostly in North America and Europe. Places are reported by each host and may be offset on purpose. No probe says nothing about no service.

notes: At least one serving satellite stood above the service angle of 25 degrees (5 degrees from 62 north) for all of the 24 hours at every latitude, pole to pole. The most were in view near 63 degrees latitude (141 on average); the fewest at any moment anywhere was 1.

Service angles as the FCC authorised them: user terminals work down to 25 degrees above the horizon below 62 degrees north, and down to 5 degrees at and above it (FCC DA 24-1193). SpaceX has asked for 20 degrees on its 400 to 500 km shells; no grant was found.

Serving satellites are taken as those between 425 and 600 km on near-circular orbits. The FCC's January 2026 order (DA 26-36) also authorises shells at 340 to 365 km, and the element sets hold about 800 satellites near 350 to 375 km. Whether those are serving or still raising cannot be told from the orbits, so they are left out and counted under Other.

Starlink's IP geolocation feed is not drawn. It lists 238 countries and territories, including ones where Starlink has no licence, and SpaceX does not say what a row means, so it is not a service-area map.
Not shown, because it is not geometry: which countries have service (the operator's availability map says), where gateways are, and how much capacity a cell has.

tables.title: Orbits in the element sets
tables.note: Grouped by inclination to the nearest half degree. Serving: 425 to 600 km and near-circular; the rest are raising, lowering or spare.
